name: Virtual machines
summary: A whole computer, carved out of a bigger physical one.
howItWorks: A hypervisor splits one physical server into several isolated machines. Each VM gets its own virtual CPUs, memory and disk, plus a full operating system that you install, patch and secure. To your software it looks exactly like a real server.
analogy: Renting a furnished apartment in a big building. The walls are yours to paint, the plumbing is shared, and everything inside your door is your responsibility.
useWhen: Lifting an existing app off an office server without rewriting it
Software that needs a specific OS, kernel module or licensed agent
Long-running workloads where you want full control over tuning
avoidWhen: Spiky traffic: you pay for the machine while it sits idle
Small teams that don’t want to own OS patching and hardening
example: A company moves its ten-year-old Windows ERP system to the cloud by copying it onto an 8-vCPU VM. Nothing in the app changes; the server just lives in a cloud data center now.

providers.oss: KVM, Proxmox, OpenStack; Vagrant for local dev VMs; Packer to build images; KubeVirt for VMs managed by Kubernetes

diagram.caption: Traffic for three different tenants lands on three VMs that share one physical server. Each VM runs its own operating system and can’t see the others.

story: Virtual machines began as a way to share one very expensive computer. At IBM’s Cambridge Scientific Center, working alongside MIT, engineers built CP-40 on a specially modified System/360 Model 40. It went into production in January 1967, giving each user a virtual machine that could run its own operating system as if it had the hardware to itself. The design became CP-67 and then IBM’s VM/370 (1972). In 1974 Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg wrote down the rules: a guest must behave as on real hardware, the monitor must stay in control, and the guest must run at nearly full speed, with most instructions running directly on the CPU.

The PC’s x86 chips broke those rules: some sensitive instructions didn’t trap to the monitor. VMware, founded in 1998 by Stanford’s Mendel Rosenblum, Diane Greene and others, got around this in VMware Workstation (1999) by rewriting problem kernel instructions on the fly. Cambridge University’s Xen (2003) took a different route, modifying the guest OS to call the hypervisor directly. In 2005 Intel and AMD added hardware support (VT-x and AMD-V), and KVM used it to turn Linux itself into a hypervisor.

Virtualization on ordinary x86 servers let one physical machine host many isolated ones, which is the basis of every public cloud: EC2 ran on Xen from 2006, and from 2017 its new instances moved to the Nitro system, whose hypervisor is based on KVM.

choices.choice: Run guest code directly; trap only the sensitive parts
choices.why: Emulating every instruction would be far too slow. Letting the CPU run ordinary instructions natively and stepping in only for privileged ones is what makes a VM nearly as fast as bare metal.

choices.choice: Binary translation when the hardware won’t help
choices.why: Since x86 couldn’t trap every sensitive instruction, VMware scanned kernel code and rewrote the problem instructions before they ran, while still running user code directly.

choices.choice: Paravirtualization: let the guest know it’s virtual
choices.why: Xen changed the guest kernel to make explicit calls to the hypervisor instead of touching hardware, which avoided costly emulation.
VT-x and AMD-V gave x86 a proper mode for guests, so a hypervisor no longer needed rewriting tricks. KVM, which turned Linux into a hypervisor, depends on them.

timeline.text: IBM’s CP-40 goes into production, running virtual machines on one System/360
VMware Workstation virtualizes the x86 PC
Xen released from the University of Cambridge
Intel VT-x and AMD-V add hardware virtualization to x86
New EC2 instances move from Xen to the KVM-based Nitro hypervisor
Broadcom completes its purchase of VMware
